# Average Age of First Kiss (and Why Yours Doesn't Matter) Every few weeks I get an email that is secretly the same email, sent by different people at strange hours. The wording varies. The question underneath never does: what's the average age of a first kiss, and am I normal? Here's the number, right at the top, because I refuse to make you scroll for it. In the United States, the average age of a first kiss is about 15. A global survey that asked twenty thousand people across thirty countries came back with 15.7. Most first kisses on this planet land somewhere between 12 and 18. That's the answer you searched for. Stay with me anyway, because that tidy little number is hiding a much stranger and much kinder truth, and the people who need it most are exactly the ones lying awake doing math against it. ## The average age of a first kiss around the world The mid-teens figure shows up again and again across separate surveys, which is about as close to consensus as kissing research gets. But the moment you sort the data by country, the idea of a single normal age falls apart: - France averages 13.5, because of course it does. - The United States sits right around 15. - Germany and the United Kingdom come in near 16. - Sweden, Norway, and Denmark hover around 17. - Japan averages 18.5. - India averages 22. Read that list again. The gap between France and India is nearly nine years. Same species, same lips, same biology. The only thing that changed was the culture wrapped around them. If normal can shift by almost a decade when you cross a border, then normal was never a law of nature. It's a local custom, like tipping. Nobody in Mumbai is seven years behind the French. They're just living under different rules about romance, privacy, and what teenagers are allowed to do on a Tuesday. And if you're wondering about gender: men average 15.4 and women 15.9. Half a year. Statistical noise. This is one scoreboard where nobody is winning anything. ## The average is the most misleading number in the room Here's a fact I love: the average American has one ovary and one testicle. Averages are like that. They describe crowds with great precision and individual people not at all. Let me show you the spread that this particular average buries. In 2018, three researchers (Lefkowitz, Wesche, and Leavitt) surveyed 738 first-year university students at a large northeastern school and asked whether they had ever kissed anyone. 14.2 percent said no. That's one in seven college students, walking around campus, never been kissed. Inside the honors college it was 32 percent. One in three. The students with the strongest transcripts were kissing latest, which should permanently retire the theory that a late first kiss means something is wrong with you. Sometimes it just means you were at the library becoming the kind of person people fall for later. Busy is a timeline too. One more split from the same study, and it's the one worth memorizing. Among students in a romantic relationship, 1 percent had never been kissed. Among single students, 22 percent. Same campus, same age, same everything. The difference isn't desirability or some invisible defect. It's opportunity. A first kiss isn't a milestone your body owes you at a certain age. It's an event that requires another person, decent timing, and a little luck. ## First kisses are trending later, everywhere If you still feel behind, I have news that should loosen the knot in your chest: the entire world is drifting in your direction. Japan has surveyed its students about romance every six years since 1974. In the most recent round, covering more than 12,000 teenagers, about one in five senior high school boys had experienced a first kiss. That's the lowest figure in the survey's fifty-year history. Girls came in at 27.5 percent, down nearly 14 points in a single six-year stretch. At the peak, back in 2005, roughly half of Japanese high schoolers had kissed someone. Japan runs the cleanest long-term data, but the pattern isn't Japanese. Pandemic-era teenagers spent formative years apart from each other. Adolescence increasingly happens through a screen, where you can flirt for three years without once standing inside kissing distance. People date later, marry later, do everything later. Which means the mental montage you're comparing yourself to, the one where everyone locked eyes at a bonfire at fifteen, was filmed decades ago. The definition of on time is being renegotiated right now, in your favor, whether you asked for it or not. ## What actually decides when a first kiss happens Strip out the mythology and the timing of a first kiss comes down to a short list, none of which is a character flaw: - **Opportunity.** Remember the 1 percent versus 22 percent split. Proximity to someone who wants to kiss you is most of the entire game. - **Temperament.** The same 2018 study found that students who hadn't kissed anyone skewed more introverted. Quieter people take longer to end up in kissing situations. That's geometry, not pathology. - **Culture.** A teenager in Paris and a teenager in Mumbai are running completely different playbooks, and both are normal where they're standing. - **Choice.** Plenty of people wait on purpose: for comfort, for the right person, for reasons that are nobody's business. A kiss you actually wanted at 22 beats a kiss you tolerated at 14 by every measure that matters. - **Luck.** Sometimes the person you wanted to kiss moved away in March. Timelines hinge on absurdly small things, and none of them are a referendum on you. Notice what's not on the list: attractiveness, worthiness, how lovable you are. The data keeps pointing at circumstances. Our brains keep insisting it's a verdict. The data is right. There's a reason the whole subject feels so enormous, by the way. Your body treats a first kiss as a genuinely major event: a flood of information about scent, taste, and touch that it cannot collect any other way. I've written about [the science of what happens when lips touch](/blog/science-of-kissing/), and the short version is that your nervous system takes kissing very seriously. It's allowed to. You're allowed to stop treating the calendar as part of it.

Whenever your first kiss arrives, the timeline stops mattering the moment lips touch. What you do next is the part people remember. Kiss Perfect Now is the complete system: the reads, the rhythm, and the habits that make any kiss feel like your hundredth.

## If your first kiss has not happened yet First: you're in enormous company, and the company grows every year. One in seven of those college freshmen. One in three honors kids. Whole generations starting later on every continent. I've written a longer letter to you specifically in [Never Been Kissed? Here's What Everyone's Afraid to Tell You](/blog/never-been-kissed/), and if tonight's search had a knot in your stomach behind it, read that next. For now, let me hand you the two most useful truths. The clock isn't measuring anything. There's no biological window for a first kiss. Nothing calcifies. Late first kisses are, if anything, systematically better than mid-teen ones: they tend to be chosen rather than stumbled into, wanted rather than performed for an audience of cafeteria observers, and conducted by someone who has met themselves. You've spent extra years becoming a specific person. Whoever gets your first kiss gets that person, not a nervous kid. The skill takes days, not years. People assume everyone who started at 15 has a decade of practice on them. What those people mostly have is a decade of unremarkable kissing. The mechanics are learnable fast, and [you can practice most of kissing before you've kissed anyone](/blog/how-to-practice-kissing/): lip care, breathing, rhythm, presence. When the moment shows up, [reading whether someone wants to kiss you](/blog/how-to-tell-if-someone-wants-to-kiss-you/) and [knowing what to do with a first kiss](/blog/how-to-kiss-someone-for-the-first-time/) will carry you further than any teenager's head start. ## If yours happened on schedule (and was terrible) A word for the other half of my readers: the ones who hit the average dead-on and are still recovering. Consider what an average-age first kiss usually looks like. Two fifteen-year-olds, combined kissing experience of zero, adrenaline at defibrillator levels, in a basement or behind a gym, occasionally with braces involved on both ends. The average age produces reliably below-average kisses. Landing on schedule bought most people nothing but an earlier awkward memory. That's the joke buried inside this whole question. The milestone everyone measures themselves against was, for most of the people who hit it, a minor traffic accident they laugh about now. If yours still stings, I've covered [what a bad first kiss means and what it doesn't](/blog/bad-first-kiss/), and the answer is: almost nothing, almost always. Nobody wins the timeline. Everybody learns the actual skill later, in private, with someone they like. The start date washes out of the data almost immediately. ## The only timeline that matters The average age of a first kiss is 15, and it's the least important fact I've ever published on this site. An average measures when a crowd started. It says nothing about how it went, what it meant, or where it led, and it has zero predictive power over the kisses still ahead of you. A first kiss isn't a deadline or a diagnosis. It's a door, and doors don't care what year you walk through them. Whether yours happened at 13, lives in your imagination under someday, or sits in your memory filed under the braces incident: you're not behind. You were never behind. There was no race. There's just the next kiss, whenever it arrives. My whole job is making sure it's a good one. ## Frequently Asked Questions ### What is the average age of a first kiss? About 15 in the United States, and 15.7 worldwide according to a survey of twenty thousand people across thirty countries. The average varies enormously by country, from roughly 13.5 in France to 22 in India, and most people have their first kiss somewhere between ages 12 and 18. ### Is it normal to have never been kissed at 16, 18, or 20? Completely normal, and more common every year. A 2018 study of 738 first-year university students found that 14.2 percent had never been kissed, and the figure rose to 32 percent inside the honors college. The strongest predictor wasn't attractiveness but simple opportunity: among students not in a relationship, 22 percent had never kissed anyone. ### Is 25 too late for a first kiss? No, and the idea of too late has no biological basis. Later first kisses tend to be chosen deliberately rather than performed under peer pressure, which usually makes them better experiences. Kissing is also a fast-learning skill: within a handful of kisses, a late starter is indistinguishable from someone who began at 14. ### Do people who have their first kiss later end up worse at kissing? No. First-kiss age reflects circumstances, culture, and opportunity, not ability. Most of what makes someone a good kisser, like presence, pacing, and reading a partner, develops through ongoing kissing, not at the first attempt, and much of it can be practiced before a first kiss ever happens.
